blocks.prompt: The Man Who Gave the Sandwich Its Name
blocks.text: A long time ago in England, there was a man named John. He was the Earl of Sandwich. That was his title, and it came from a little town by the sea called Sandwich. The story goes that John did not want to stop working to eat. He asked for cold meat tucked between two slices of bread. Then he could hold his food in one hand and keep going. People saw it and said, I will have the same as Sandwich. The name stuck. So the sandwich is not named after bread or meat. It is named after a man, and that man was named after a town.

blocks.prompt: Two Slices and a Big Idea
blocks.text: Before the sandwich had a name, people were already eating one. More than two thousand years ago, a teacher named Hillel wrapped lamb and bitter herbs inside flat bread so he could eat them together. In the Middle Ages, people in Europe used thick slices of stale bread as plates. They called them trenchers. The bread soaked up the juices from the meat, and at the end of the meal the soggy trencher was given to the poor or to the dogs. The word sandwich came much later. In the 1700s, an English nobleman named John Montagu held the title Earl of Sandwich. He liked to eat cold meat between two slices of bread while he stayed busy at his table. His friends began asking for the same thing, and they called it by his title. The town of Sandwich in England had given the man his name. The man gave the food its name. The food kept it.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Gluten is what makes bread stretchy and strong
Butter waterproofs bread against wet fillings
Toasting browns bread through the Maillard reaction
Louis-Camille Maillard studied that reaction in 1912

blocks.prompt: Why the Bread Goes on the Outside
blocks.text: A sandwich looks simple. It is not. Every good sandwich is solving a problem, and the problem is your hands. Bread works as a wrapper because of gluten. When flour meets water, two proteins in the flour link up into a stretchy web. Yeast fills that web with bubbles of gas, and baking sets it hard. What comes out is a solid that is also soft: strong enough to hold a load of wet filling, gentle enough to bite through. No plate, no fork, no napkin needed. Bread has one weakness. It drinks. Tomato juice, oil, and dressing soak straight into it, and a soaked slice tears. Cooks have fought this for centuries. The old trick is fat. A thin layer of butter or mayonnaise on the inside face of the bread does almost nothing for flavor and everything for waterproofing, because fat and water refuse to mix. That is also why the wet things belong in the middle of the stack and the dry things belong against the bread. Toasting helps too. Heat drives water out of the surface of the slice and starts a chemical reaction between the sugars and the proteins in the crust. That reaction is named for Louis-Camille Maillard, the French chemist who studied it in 1912. It is what turns bread brown and gives toast its smell. A toasted slice is drier, stiffer, and much harder to drown.

answers: food that is wet or greasy normally needs a plate and a fork; bread lets you hold it instead
fat and water do not mix, so the butter blocks the liquid from soaking in
(inference: the dry filling sits against the bread and shields it from the juice)
(inference: butter both slices and toast the bread)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Otto Rohwedder spent about sixteen years on the bread slicer
The first machine ran in Chillicothe, Missouri, in July 1928
By 1933 roughly 80 percent of US bread was sold pre-sliced
The United States banned sliced bread in January 1943
The ban was lifted about two months later

blocks.prompt: The Greatest Thing
blocks.text: For most of its life, the sandwich was a rich person's snack and a poor person's lunch, and both were made by hand. Bread came from the baker as a whole loaf. Cutting even slices off it took a sharp knife, a steady hand, and time. A crooked slice made a crooked sandwich. Bread was the one part of lunch that still needed a blade. Otto Rohwedder thought a machine could do it better. He was a jeweler by trade, born in Iowa, and he spent about sixteen years on the problem. The hard part was not the cutting. It was what happened afterward. A sliced loaf dries out fast and falls apart on the shelf, so grocers refused to stock it. Rohwedder's answer was to slice the loaf and wrap it in the same motion. His machine first ran in a bakery in Chillicothe, Missouri, in July 1928. Within five years, most bread sold in America came pre-sliced. The effect was bigger than convenience. Uniform slices made the sandwich something a child could build without a knife, which is one reason peanut butter and jelly became the standard American lunch. Toasters suddenly had a job. Sales of bread went up, because a slice is easy to eat and easy to eat again. The phrase the greatest thing since sliced bread comes from this moment, and people meant it. In January 1943, in the middle of the war, the United States banned sliced bread. The official reasons were saving wax paper and steel. The public reaction was loud and immediate, and the ban was lifted after about two months. A country at war, rationing meat and gasoline without much complaint, would not give up its slices. It got them back in March.

6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Man Who Gave the Sandwich Its Name

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Sandwich, Kent: Old English for a trading place on the sand
James Cook named Hawaii the Sandwich Islands in 1778
The card-table story was printed in 1772, secondhand
Montagu ran the British navy three separate times
Banh mi uses the baguette left behind by French colonizers
The Cuban sandwich is pressed flat while it is hot

blocks.prompt: The Sandwich: A Technology for Eating Without Stopping
blocks.text: The sandwich is not a recipe. It is a piece of engineering, and like most good engineering it disappears into the thing it solves. Start with the problem. Food that is hot, wet, or greasy demands a plate, a utensil, a table, and a pause. That pause is expensive. It has always been expensive, for a soldier, a field hand, a gambler, a clerk, and a kid with fifteen minutes of recess left. The sandwich abolishes the pause. It wraps the wet part in the dry part and hands you your lunch as a solid object. What it really buys you is not convenience. It is time. People solved this long before anyone named it. Over two thousand years ago, Hillel the Elder is said to have folded lamb and bitter herbs into flat bread at Passover, and Jewish families still eat a version of it today. Medieval European kitchens served meat on trenchers, thick slabs of day-old bread that worked as edible plates and were handed to the poor once the meal was over. Every one of these is the same idea. Bread is the only common food that is strong, dry, absorbent, and edible all at once. The name arrived in England in the 1700s, and it arrived attached to a person. John Montagu, the fourth Earl of Sandwich, held the title of a small port town in Kent whose Old English name means roughly a trading place on the sand. Montagu ate cold meat between bread while he worked, and the men around him started ordering the same thing by his title. Here the popular story and the historical record disagree. The version everyone repeats says he would not leave the card table. That account was printed in 1772 by a French visitor to London who had heard it secondhand. Montagu's biographer argues the truth is duller and more likely: he ran the British navy, sat at his desk through very long days, and wanted to eat without putting down his papers. Both versions agree on the point that matters. Somebody important refused to stop, and the food adapted to him. Then the sandwich went industrial. Otto Rohwedder's bread slicer reached a Missouri bakery in 1928, and within five years most American bread was sold pre-sliced. That single machine turned sandwich making into something a seven-year-old could do unsupervised, which is roughly when peanut butter and jelly took over the American lunchbox. When the government banned sliced bread in January 1943 to conserve wax paper, the country complained so loudly that the ban was gone by March. The strongest evidence that the sandwich is a solution and not a fashion is that it kept getting reinvented by people who had never heard of the Earl. Vietnam took the baguette left behind by French colonizers, filled it with pork, pickled carrot, and cilantro, and made the banh mi. Mexico built the torta on a bolillo roll. Cuban workers in Florida pressed ham, roast pork, and pickles flat between hot plates. Nobody was copying England. They were all answering the same question, and bread kept giving the same answer.

(at The strongest evidence that the sandwich is a solution and not a fashion; the author stops narrating and starts proving)
